summary: For ages 12–13: build an explicit, nested-scale model of DNA, genes and chromosomes (cell → nucleus → chromosome → one long DNA molecule → a gene as a section of that DNA), fix the key facts (double helix with base pairs; 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs; a gene codes for a protein, which in turn affects a characteristic), and teach the contested discovery story (X-ray crystallography at King's College London by Franklin and by Wilkins; Photo 51 was taken in Franklin's lab by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, and Wilkins showed it to Watson without Franklin's knowledge; this evidence helped Watson and Crick build the double-helix model). The core learning objective is holding this multi-level structure in mind and reasoning about part-whole and scale relationships, plus discussing evidence, credit and the nature of science.
misconceptions: Thinking a chromosome contains many separate pieces of DNA, rather than being ONE long coiled DNA molecule.
Treating genes, DNA and chromosomes as three separate kinds of thing rather than nested parts of one structure (gene = section of DNA; DNA coils into a chromosome).
Believing DNA/genes are only in special cells (e.g. sex cells or blood) rather than in the nucleus of nearly every body cell.
Confusing a gene (a section of DNA coding for a characteristic) with a whole chromosome, or with a single 'trait' with no physical basis.
Assuming Watson and Crick discovered DNA's structure alone, unaware that Franklin's and Wilkins's X-ray evidence was essential.
Muddling the numbers — e.g. thinking humans have 23 chromosomes rather than 46 (23 pairs).

activities.title: Zoom down the scales: from cell to a single gene
steps: Start from a single body cell and work inwards one level at a time: cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA molecule → gene.

At the chromosome level, watch (or trace, in a drawn/animated version) a single chromosome unwind into one single, very long twisted-ladder DNA molecule. (The familiar X shape is a chromosome that has been copied before the cell divides: two identical DNA molecules joined together, so each arm of the X unwinds into its own DNA molecule.)
Along the unwound helix, identify and highlight a short stretch and label it: 'a gene — a section of DNA that codes for a protein (which in turn affects a characteristic).'
Record the key numbers at the right level: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs in a human body cell; the double helix has two strands with base pairs as rungs.
Cross-link the helix view to a karyotype image showing the 23 pairs.
activities.insight: A chromosome is not a bag of separate DNA pieces — an uncopied chromosome IS one enormously long, tightly coiled DNA molecule (the X shape seen before division is two identical copies joined together); and a gene is not separate from DNA but a stretch OF it. The levels nest inside one another in scale order.

activities.title: Handle the double helix in three dimensions
steps: Rotate and inspect a double helix (physical model, 3D on-screen model, or built twisted-ladder) to see the two strands twisting around each other with base pairs as rungs.
Unspool a 3D or physical chromosome model into its DNA thread to feel how a huge length coils into a compact structure.
Point out complementary base pairs at model level (rungs pair up) without going into GCSE-level biochemistry.
Zoom in on one gene segment and relate it back to the whole helix.
activities.insight: The helix is genuinely three-dimensional — two strands, base pairs, a twist — and extreme coiling is how a very long molecule fits inside a tiny nucleus.

activities.title: Talk to Rosalind Franklin about Photo 51
steps: Interview (in role-play, or with a prepared in-role script) Rosalind Franklin or Maurice Wilkins about what X-ray crystallography is and what Photo 51 showed.
Ask how that evidence fed into the model Watson and Crick built.
Probe the fairness of credit: who provided the evidence, who built the model, and how recognition was shared.
Summarise each of the four scientists' contributions in your own words.
activities.insight: DNA's structure was discovered through real collaborative and contested science: X-ray evidence from King's College London (Wilkins's work, and Franklin's, including Photo 51, taken by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling and shown to Watson by Wilkins without her knowledge) provided key evidence for the Watson–Crick model, raising genuine questions about evidence, credit and how science works.

activities.title: Build and consolidate the hierarchy
steps: Assemble the hierarchy by nesting: place a gene inside a DNA molecule, inside a chromosome, inside the nucleus, inside the cell — in correct scale order (drag-and-nest, cut-out cards, or a drawn diagram).
Order the five levels from smallest to largest: DNA base, gene, chromosome, nucleus, cell.
Match each scientist (Watson, Crick, Franklin, Wilkins) to their contribution.
Fill in the numbers: human body cells have ___ chromosomes in ___ pairs (46; 23).
State in a sentence what a gene is and what it codes for.
Answer a check question such as: does a chromosome contain many separate DNA pieces, or is it one long coiled DNA molecule?
activities.insight: The facts, numbers, part-whole nesting and discovery roles can be stated accurately and in the correct order.

activities.title: Why do identical-DNA cells differ? (differential expression)
steps: Consider the claim: 'A skin cell contains the genes for skin, and a muscle cell contains the genes for muscle — that's why they differ.' Decide whether it is right and explain.
Explain what each cell actually contains in terms of DNA, genes and chromosomes.
Answer the probe: if every body cell has the same DNA, why doesn't a muscle cell look and behave like a skin cell?
State what a gene codes for and how that links to cell differences.
activities.insight: Nearly every body cell carries the SAME complete genome (all 46 chromosomes, all the genes); cell types differ because they USE (express) different genes, not because they hold different genes.

checkQuestion: A student says: 'A skin cell contains the genes for skin, and a muscle cell contains the genes for muscle — that's why they turn out different.' Is that right? Explain what each of these cells actually contains, in terms of DNA, genes and chromosomes.
checkAnswer: No. Nearly every body cell contains the SAME complete set of DNA — all 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), all the genes. Skin and muscle cells differ because they USE (express) different genes, not because they hold different ones. The hierarchy: DNA coils up into chromosomes inside the nucleus of the cell, and a gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.
